newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Strike spectre looms over BA.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Strike spectre looms over BA.

text.p: British Airways looked set for a turbulent ride on Wednesday after an overwhelming majority of its cabin crew voted to strike to settle a five-month fight over pay and conditions.
The T&G union, representing around three quarters of BA's mainline cabin crew, said 75 percent of 9,000 staff balloted took part in the vote. Of those, 73 percent backed strike action.

The union said it would decide on Monday what type of action to take, only one day before BA faces another potentially damaging ballot when 9,000 ground staff vote over the controversial sale of its catering unit.
Investors took fright at the strike threat, which BA chief executive Bob Ayling called "regrettable but not surprising", and BA shares dropped 10.5 pence to 690p.
But they pared some losses later after the carrier vowed to implement contingency plans to maintain services and analysts played down the escalating dispute.

"Obviously a strike in the summer season would be pretty bad news...but this time last year the pilots were threatening to strike and it was called off before it got started. I expect the shares to remain weak while we remain in this posturing stage," one analyst said.
Experts said BA had a buffer period because unions must give seven days' notice ahead of any strike action, which must be taken within 24 days of the ballot.
The airline has already hinted it has emergency measures in place, including offering jobs to others to replace striking employees.
T&G regional officer Eddie McDermott savaged the contingency plan as the creation of a "scab army" and predicted services would suffer if new personnel were drafted in.

But BA said services would be maintained, noting that its European and domestic services from London's Gatwick airport and services operated by British Airways Regional from the UK regions were not involved in the ballot. Also, staff in its franchise and alliance partners were not part of the vote, BA said.
It made no mention of operations at Heathrow Airport, London's major hub.
BA called the strike ballot absurd, considering that the wages package had already been given the green light by the Cabin Crew 89 union, which represents a quarter of BA's mainline cabin staff.

"How do you reach agreement with a union that walks away from the table, particularly when the other union has voted overwhelmingly 'yes'? The outcome of this ballot is regrettable especially as the deal is good for staff," Ayling said.

BA agreed a deal with Cabin Crew 89 comprising a basic wage rise of between 14.2 percent and 24 percent, with higher pensionable salaries and better profit-sharing terms, sickness and maternity leave benefits.

BA has promised to guarantee that cabin crew would not be any worse off under the new pay restructuring agreement, which is part of the carrier's drive to boost efficiency amid a frantic race to forge new alliances worldwide.
